blocks.text: Quick verdict

Decodo is the simpler and usually cheaper choice for US and Western European scraping: 10 GB costs $35 against $50 on SOAX's Sandbox for US traffic, and 100 GB costs $275 against about $300 on SOAX Builder. SOAX is the better choice for mobile-first work, ad verification and traffic in its cheaper Tier 2 and Tier 3 countries, and for workloads that need UDP or QUIC. If unused credits expiring after 60 days worries you, Decodo's PAYG option is the safer fit for bursty demand.

Decodo and SOAX are two of the most capable mid-market networks, both with pools above 100 million advertised IPs and city-level targeting. Their pricing logic is completely different. Decodo charges a published rate per gigabyte regardless of where your traffic exits. SOAX charges prepaid credits whose burn rate depends on your plan and on the exit country's tier, and those credits expire after 60 days. This comparison shows when each model is cheaper and which features break the tie.

blocks.text: Decodo in 2026: what you get

Decodo is the 2024 rebrand of Smartproxy, one of the most popular mid-market providers. Its residential network is advertised at 115 million IPs across 195+ locations, and independent benchmarks put its success rate around 99.9% with sub-second response times. Every plan includes the full pool plus city, state, ZIP and ASN targeting, and the dashboard is one of the easiest to set up. Decodo also sells datacenter, ISP and mobile proxies and a family of scraping APIs.

Strengths: Large 115M+ pool at a mid-market price; Near-perfect success rates in independent tests; Clean, fast self-service onboarding; Scraping APIs available when raw proxies are not enough. Weak spots: Plan traffic does not roll over; Published pricing stops at 100 GB; beyond that you need a quote; More expensive per GB than budget brands.
SOAX in 2026: what you get

SOAX is a residential and mobile specialist known for granular filtering. Its 2026 pricing replaced fixed GB bundles with plans (Sandbox, Builder, Team, Scale, Enterprise) that include credits, and the credit burn rate depends on the exit country's tier. That makes SOAX cheap for some geographies and expensive for low-volume US work. The network is large (155M residential, 33M mobile advertised) and supports protocols few competitors offer, including UDP and QUIC.

Strengths: Residential and mobile on one balance; UDP and QUIC support alongside SOCKS5; Large pool with city and ISP targeting on every plan; Cheap traffic for Tier 2 and Tier 3 countries. Weak spots: Credits expire after 60 days; US traffic is expensive on small plans; Datacenter and ISP proxies were discontinued.
Pricing: Decodo vs SOAX

Decodo sells residential traffic at $4/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, or on monthly plans: 3 GB for $11.25 ($3.75/GB), 10 GB for $35, 25 GB at $3.25/GB, 50 GB for $150 and 100 GB for $275 ($2.75/GB). Top-ups are billed at your plan's rate, so you are not pushed into the next tier.

SOAX bills prepaid credits. For US (Tier 1) traffic, the no-fee Sandbox plan costs $5/GB, Builder ($200/month) $3/GB, Team ($500/month) $2.20/GB, and Scale ($1,500/month) $1.50/GB; cheaper countries cost less (Tier 3 from $2/GB on Sandbox). Credits expire 60 days after purchase, and SOAX counts traffic in both directions.

At 10 GB a month, Decodo is the cheaper option at about $35 against $50 for SOAX, roughly 30% less. For a 100 GB month, Decodo costs about $275 while SOAX costs about $300, so Decodo saves around 8%. Both Decodo and SOAX work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

By advertised size, SOAX (155M residential + 33M mobile) is about 1.3x larger than Decodo (115M+). Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, Decodo lists 195+ countries and SOAX lists 195. On targeting, Decodo offers country, state, city, ZIP and ASN, while SOAX offers country, region, city and ISP; ASN and ZIP on Scale plans.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, Decodo offers rotating or sticky sessions with configurable duration, and SOAX offers rotating or sticky; mobile sessions up to 60 minutes. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?
General web scraping: Decodo. Decodo has the edge here. Why: a large pool and near-perfect benchmark success rates. How SOAX compares: a large pool and its own error headers help debugging.

SERP and rank tracking: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Decodo: a dedicated SERP scraping API plus city targeting. SOAX: city and ISP targeting for local results. Let price and the countries you need decide.

Social media and multi-account management: SOAX wins. The deciding factor for SOAX: mobile IPs on the same balance as residential. The limitation on the Decodo side: sticky sessions, sub-users and an easy dashboard.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Decodo: ZIP targeting and a ready-made e-commerce API. SOAX: granular location filters. Let price and the countries you need decide.
Ad verification and geo-testing: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: ISP, ASN and carrier-level targeting. How Decodo compares: wide coverage with city and ASN targeting.

Tight budgets: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Decodo: it is mid-priced, not cheap. With SOAX: cheap in Tier 3 countries but pricey for small US jobs. Run the same small test on both before committing.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Decodo: Free trial (about 100 MB) on residential. SOAX: Paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99. Verification and payment rules differ too. Decodo: Light KYC; checks on some targets. SOAX: Verification for postpaid and enterprise terms. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Decodo and SOAX before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Decodo vs SOAX faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Decodo: free trial (about 100 MB) on residential; SOAX: paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Decodo comes out ahead in 1, SOAX in 2, and 3 are ties. That makes SOAX the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Decodo is strongest for small and mid-size scraping teams, while SOAX is strongest for mobile-first work such as app testing and social platforms. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.

Mixed workloads that may grow into scraping APIs
SOAX is the better pick for:

Teams targeting cheaper Tier 2/3 countries
